content: 1. Efavirenz plasma concentrations can be influenced by substrates, inhibitors, or inducers of the CYP3A enzyme. Similarly, efavirenz can alter the plasma concentrations of drugs metabolized by CYP3A or CYP2B6 enzymes. 2. Efavirenz (SUSTIVA) should not be used as a single agent to treat HIV-1 infection or added as the sole agent to a failing antiretroviral regimen. Resistance develops rapidly when efavirenz is used as monotherapy. When selecting new antiretroviral agents to combine with efavirenz, the potential for viral cross-resistance should be considered. 3. Co-administration of SUSTIVA with ATRIPLA (a combination of efavirenz, emtricitabine, and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) is not recommended unless necessary for dose adjustment, such as when used with rifampin, because efavirenz is already an active ingredient in ATRIPLA. 4. Serious psychiatric adverse events, including severe depression, suicidal ideation, non-fatal suicide attempts, aggressive behavior, paranoid reactions, and psychosis-like symptoms, have been reported in patients treated with SUSTIVA. These symptoms may occur at any time during treatment. Patients with a history of psychiatric illness, injection drug use, or those receiving psychiatric medications at the start of therapy may be at increased risk. In some cases, these symptoms have led to treatment discontinuation. Rare postmarketing reports of suicide, delusions, and psychosis-like behavior have been documented, but a causal relationship to efavirenz use cannot be definitively established. Patients experiencing serious psychiatric symptoms should seek immediate medical evaluation to determine if the symptoms are related to efavirenz and whether the risks of continued therapy outweigh the benefits. 5. Nervous system symptoms, such as dizziness, impaired concentration, and drowsiness, are common with efavirenz treatment. These symptoms typically begin within the first or second day of therapy and generally resolve after 2-4 weeks. After 4 weeks, the prevalence of moderate-to-severe nervous system symptoms ranges from 5% to 9% in patients treated with efavirenz-containing regimens. Patients should be informed that these symptoms are likely to improve with continued therapy and are not predictive of more severe psychiatric symptoms. Taking the medication at bedtime may improve tolerability. Patients should avoid hazardous tasks, such as driving or operating machinery, if they experience these symptoms. Long-term data suggest that the incidence of new-onset nervous system symptoms beyond 24 weeks of therapy is similar to that observed in control groups. 6. Efavirenz may cause fetal harm when administered during the first trimester of pregnancy. Women receiving SUSTIVA should avoid pregnancy, and effective barrier contraception should always be used in combination with other contraceptive methods. Due to the long half-life of efavirenz, adequate contraceptive measures should be maintained for 12 weeks after discontinuation of the drug. Women of childbearing potential should undergo pregnancy testing before starting SUSTIVA. If efavirenz is used during the first trimester or if a patient becomes pregnant while taking it, the patient should be informed of the potential risk to the fetus. SUSTIVA should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus, such as in cases where no alternative therapeutic options are available. 7. Rash is a common side effect of efavirenz, typically presenting as mild-to-moderate maculopapular eruptions within the first two weeks of therapy (median onset: 11 days). Most rashes resolve within one month (median duration: 16 days) without discontinuing therapy. Severe rashes, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and erythema multiforme, have been reported. Pediatric patients may experience a higher incidence of rash, with some cases being severe. Prophylaxis with antihistamines before initiating therapy in pediatric patients may be considered. SUSTIVA should be discontinued in patients who develop severe rashes with blistering, desquamation, mucosal involvement, or fever. Antihistamines and/or corticosteroids may improve tolerability and hasten rash resolution. Alternative therapy should be considered for patients with life-threatening cutaneous reactions. 8. Monitoring of liver enzymes is recommended before and during treatment with efavirenz, especially in patients with underlying hepatic disease (e.g., hepatitis B or C), marked transaminase elevations, or those receiving other hepatotoxic medications. Rare cases of hepatic failure have been reported, even in patients without pre-existing liver disease or identifiable risk factors. Persistent elevations of serum transaminases greater than five times the upper limit of normal should prompt a careful assessment of the risks and benefits of continued therapy. 9. Convulsions have been observed in adult and pediatric patients receiving efavirenz, particularly in those with a known history of seizures. Caution is advised in patients with a seizure history. Periodic monitoring of plasma levels may be necessary for patients taking concomitant anticonvulsant medications metabolized by the liver, such as phenytoin and phenobarbital. 10. Efavirenz therapy has been associated with increases in total cholesterol and triglyceride levels. Lipid testing should be performed before initiating therapy and periodically during treatment. 11. Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported in patients treated with combination antiretroviral therapy, including efavirenz. During the initial phase of treatment, patients with improving immune systems may develop an inflammatory response to residual or indolent opportunistic infections, necessitating further evaluation and treatment. Autoimmune disorders, such as Graves’ disease, polymyositis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome, have also been reported in the context of immune reconstitution, with variable onset times that can occur months after starting therapy. 12. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat, including central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, and a cushingoid appearance, has been observed in patients receiving antiretroviral therapy. The mechanism and long-term consequences of these events are not fully understood, and a causal relationship has not been established.
